items.actClause:
AN ACT to amend the public health law, in relation to school potable water
testing
items.memo:
BILL NUMBER: S2122

SPONSOR: RIVERA
 
TITLE OF BILL:

An act to amend the public health law, in relation to school potable
water testing

 
PURPOSE:

This bill would expand water testing in schools, including increasing
testing frequency, removing testing exemptions, setting action levels,
and increasing disclosure of information.

 
SUMMARY OF SPECIFIC PROVISIONS:

Section 1: Amends Public Health Law (PHL) 1110 to:  * Change required
school water testing for lead from "periodic" to annual;

* Require that tap water provided by school districts be free to school
occupants;

* Remove exemptions for certain schools from testing;

* Set the lead action level at 0.005 milligrams per liter;

* Require that laboratory reports be made public as part of existing
disclosure requirements for testing results; and

* Require training of those responsible for the testing. Section 2:
Provides the effective date.

 
JUSTIFICATION:

The purpose of this bill is to ensure that drinking water in schools is
safe and free of lead contamination. Children are particularly vulner-
able to the harmful effects of lead, so much so that experts from the
American Academy of Pediatrics, the Centers for Disease Control and
Prevention, and the World Health Organization, agree that there is no
safe level of lead for children. High lead levels in children can bring
lifetime problems including reduced cognitive function, learning disa-
bilities, and aggressive behavior.

Data from the first round of lead testing in schools under New York's
landmark 2016 law demonstrate that our school children are drink- ing
water that contains lead. More than 82% of public schools reported at
least one drinking water tap that exceeded the action level, current- ly
set in regulation at 0.015 milligrams per liter - Washington, DC, Illi-
nois, and Vermont are all lower at 0.004 or 0.005, while the Ameri- can
Academy of Pediatrics recommends 0.001.

Current law allows exemptions from lead testing for schools deemed "lead
free" under federal requirements. However, the federal definition of
"lead free" allows up to 0.25% of lead in pipe materials to be lead;
federal law from 1986 to 2014 allowed up to 8% lead in "lead-free"
plumbing; and there were no federal restrictions before 1986. The deter-
mination of a school as being "lead free" is no guarantee of safety and
should not allow an exemption from testing.

This bill would make several improvements to New York's existing program
by reducing the action level; requiring annual (rather than "periodic")
testing; removing waivers and exemptions for certain schools; requiring
lab reports to be posted online; and requiring training for school
personnel or contractors involved in testing.  These measures will
further protect our children from the devastating effects of lead
contamination.

 
PRIOR LEGISLATIVE HISTORY:

2019-2020: S7268/A9545 Gottfried

 
FISCAL IMPLICATIONS:

Additional school funding would be required to support additional test-
ing and remediation efforts.

 
EFFECTIVE DATE:

BILL NUMBER: S2122A

SPONSOR: RIVERA
 
TITLE OF BILL:

An act to amend the public health law, in relation to school potable
water testing

 
PURPOSE OR GENERAL IDEA OF BILL:

This bill would expand water testing in schools, including increasing
testing frequency, removing testing exemptions, and lowering lead
levels.

 
SUMMARY OF SPECIFIC PROVISIONS:

Section. 1: Amends Public Health Law 1.110 to:

*Change required school water testing for lead from "periodic" to trien-
nial (once every three years);
*Require that tap water provided by school districts be free to school
occupants;
*Remove exemptions for certain schools from testing;
*Set the lead action level at 0.005 milligrams per liter;
*Require that laboratory reports be made public as part of existing
disclosure requirements for testing results; and
*Provide remediation funding through clean water infrastructure programs

Section 2: Effective date

 
JUSTIFICATION:

The purpose of this bill is to ensure that drinking water in schools is

able to the harmful effects of lead, so much so that the experts from
the American Academy of Pediatrics, the Centers for Disease Control and
Prevention, and the World Health Organization agree that there is no
safe level of lead for children. High lead levels in children can bring
lifetime problems including reduced cognitive function, learning disa-
bilities, and aggressive behavior. The data from the first round of lead
testing in schools under New York's landmark 2016 law demonstrate that
our school children are drinking water that contains lead. More than 82
of public schools reported at least one drinking water tap that exceeded
the action level, currently set in regulation at 0.015 milligrams per
liter - Washington, DC, Illinois, and Vermont are all lower at 0.004 or
0.005, while the American Academy of Pediatrics recommends 0.001.
Current law allows exemptions from lead testing for schools deemed "lead
free" under federal requirements.  However, the federal definition of
"lead free" allows up to 0.25 of lead in pipe materials to be lead;
federal law from 1986 to 2014 allowed up to lead in "lead-free" plumb-
ing; and there were no federal restrictions before 1986. The past deem-
ing of a school as "lead free" is no guarantee of safety and should not
allow an exemption from testing.

This bill would make several improvements to New York's existing program
by reducing the action level; requiring triennial (rather than "period-
ic") testing; removing waivers and exemptions for certain schools; and
requiring lab reports to be posted online. These measures will further
protect our children from the devastating effects of lead contamination.
Finally, the amended version of the bill adds a funding mechanism by
authorizing use of clean water infrastructure funds.

 
PRIOR LEGISLATIVE HISTORY:

2020: S7268/A9545

 
FISCAL IMPLICATIONS:

Funding support through clean water infrastructure program

 
EFFECTIVE DATE:
One year after it shall have become a law

approvalMessage.text:
APPROVAL MEMORANDUM - No. 131 Chapter 771
 
       MEMORANDUM filed with Senate Bill Number 2122-A, entitled:
 
    "AN  ACT to amend the public health law, in relation to school pota-
        ble water testing"
 
    APPROVED
 
  This bill would update the School Safe Drinking Water Act of  2016  by
setting  a lead action level of 5 parts per billion (ppb) in statute, as
well as removing  exemptions  for  buildings  deemed  "lead-free"  under
federal  law,  requiring  triennial testing and requiring the posting of
lead testing lab reports on a school's website.
 
  The provisions of this bill are significant and will help protect  our
children  from  the  dangers of lead poisoning. In establishing the 5ppb
standard in law, New York will be joining three  other  states  and  the
District  of  Columbia  with  the lowest allowable lead levels in school
drinking water in the nation. Even those  buildings  deemed  "lead-free"
under existing federal law may still contain 0.2%-0.25% lead in drinking
water  pipes and fixtures. Further, lead contamination in system service
lines can cause significant lead in drinking water, even where  internal
pipes  and  fixtures  are not leeching. This is why New York continually
requires testing, and this bill would increase that testing frequency.
 
  It is also important that parents and communities know exactly what is
in their school drinking water, which is why this bill will require  lab
reports  to  be posted on school websites. Public transparency is vital,
especially when dealing with children's health. Remediation required  by
this  bill  will  be paid for from the existing funds within the State's
Clean Water Infrastructure Act.
 
  I have reached an agreement with the Legislature to  make  changes  to
this  legislation  and  ensure  that  the Commissioner of Health retains
flexibility to provide waivers to prevent unnecessary repeat testing  of
fixtures  that consistently test below the action level, and ensure that
schools use the State and Federal drinking  water  funds  available  for
this  purpose  to  conduct  testing  and remediation required under this
bill.
 
  On that basis, I am signing this bill.
 
  The bill is approved.                          (signed) KATHY HOCHUL
 
                                ______

summary: Relates to standards for and testing of potable water in school buildings; eliminates certain exemptions; sets minimum standards; permits building aid for remediation measures.
